title: Tizanidine and Alcohol: Blood Pressure, Sedation, and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on tizanidine (Zanaflex)? Why it stacks with alcohol on sedation and blood pressure, how long it lasts, risky drug combinations, and 911 signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on tizanidine (Zanaflex)? How it stacks with alcohol on blood pressure and sedation, how long it lasts, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** tizanidine (brand name Zanaflex) and alcohol are a poor combination, and the safest plan is not to drink while you take it. Tizanidine is different from most muscle relaxers. Besides making you sleepy, it lowers your blood pressure, sometimes a lot. Alcohol does both of those things too, and it also raises the amount of tizanidine in your blood. Put together, the result can be heavy drowsiness, dizziness, and fainting when you stand up. This guide explains why the two clash, how long tizanidine stays in your system, which other drugs make the picture much worse, and the warning signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink while you're taking tizanidine unless your prescriber has told you it's okay for you, and then follow their limits. Never take a dose to "settle down" after drinking. If you've had alcohol and you're due a dose, ask your pharmacist whether to skip it. Stand up slowly. Don't drive or use machinery after combining them. And don't stop tizanidine suddenly just so you can drink, because quitting abruptly can cause a rebound jump in blood pressure and heart rate.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking** if you take tizanidine, especially if you also take blood pressure medicine, an opioid, a benzodiazepine, gabapentin, a sleep aid, or an antidepressant, or if you have liver or kidney problems. **Call 911** if someone who has mixed tizanidine and alcohol faints and doesn't come round quickly, is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or shallowly, has a very slow or irregular heartbeat, is confused or hallucinating, or has hit their head in a fall.

## Why Tizanidine and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Tizanidine is a prescription drug used mainly for **spasticity**, the stiff, tight muscles that come with conditions like multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, stroke, and some brain injuries. Doctors also prescribe it off-label for muscle spasms and some pain and sleep problems. It comes as tablets and capsules, both sold as Zanaflex and as generics.

Most muscle relaxers work by generally slowing down the brain. Tizanidine works in a more specific way, and that's the key to understanding the alcohol problem.

### It's a cousin of a blood pressure drug

Tizanidine is an **alpha-2 adrenergic agonist**. In plain words, it switches on a type of receptor in the brain and spinal cord that acts like a brake on the "fight or flight" nervous system. Pressing that brake does three things at once:

1. **It relaxes muscles.** It reduces the nerve signals in the spinal cord that keep muscles tight.
2. **It makes you sleepy.** The same braking action in the brain causes drowsiness, which is one of the most common side effects.
3. **It lowers blood pressure and slows the heart.** Tizanidine is chemically and functionally related to **clonidine**, a drug that's used specifically to treat high blood pressure. Tizanidine is weaker on blood pressure than clonidine, but the effect is real and is a main safety warning on its label.

### What alcohol adds on top

Alcohol hits the same three areas from different directions:

- **Extra sedation.** Alcohol slows the brain through its own pathways, mainly by boosting the calming chemical GABA. The US prescribing information for tizanidine says the depressant effects of tizanidine and alcohol are **additive**, meaning they stack.
- **Extra blood pressure drop.** Alcohol widens blood vessels, and in the hours after drinking it can lower blood pressure, especially when you stand up. It also dehydrates you, which makes blood pressure drops worse.
- **More tizanidine in your blood.** This is the part that surprises people. According to the Zanaflex prescribing information, alcohol raised the total amount of tizanidine in the blood by about 20% and its peak level by about 15% in a study, and this came with more tizanidine side effects. So a drink doesn't just sit next to your usual dose. It effectively turns your usual dose into a slightly bigger one.

That combination of three overlapping effects is why this pairing gets a stricter warning than many other alcohol and medication combinations.

### The blood pressure part most articles skip

Many articles lump all muscle relaxers together under "they make you drowsy." With tizanidine, the bigger day-to-day danger is often **orthostatic hypotension**, which means a sudden drop in blood pressure when you stand up. You get up from the couch or out of bed, your blood pressure doesn't adjust fast enough, and you feel lightheaded, your vision greys out, or you faint.

The tizanidine label describes this blood pressure lowering as dose-related. It tends to start within about an hour of a dose and is strongest a couple of hours after it. Alcohol taken in that same window pushes in the same direction. Fainting itself is usually brief, but the fall is what hurts people: head injuries, broken wrists, and broken hips, especially in older adults.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

The prescribing information is the most reliable source here, and it is fairly direct on several points.

**Alcohol raises tizanidine levels and stacks with its sedation.** As described above, the label reports that alcohol increased tizanidine exposure and side effects, and that the central nervous system depressant effects are additive. The patient guidance is to avoid alcohol or ask your doctor first.

**Low blood pressure is a main warning.** The label warns about hypotension (low blood pressure), including fainting, and advises caution when tizanidine is used with blood pressure medicines. It also says tizanidine should not be used together with other alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine or guanfacine.

**Sedation is common.** Drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and weakness are among the most frequently reported side effects in clinical trials. The label advises against driving or doing dangerous tasks until you know how the drug affects you.

**It can affect the liver.** Tizanidine has been linked to raised liver enzymes and, rarely, serious liver injury. The label recommends liver blood tests before starting and during treatment, and caution in people with liver problems. Alcohol is also hard on the liver, which is one more reason not to pile them together.

**Some drugs are forbidden with it.** Tizanidine is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called **CYP1A2**. Drugs that strongly block this enzyme can make tizanidine levels shoot up several times higher than normal, causing dangerous drops in blood pressure and heavy sedation. Because of that, the label says tizanidine must not be taken with **fluvoxamine** (an antidepressant, brand name Luvox) or **ciprofloxacin** (an antibiotic, brand name Cipro). It also advises avoiding or using caution with a list of other CYP1A2 blockers, including some heart rhythm drugs, some other antibiotics and antivirals, cimetidine, and birth control pills, which can raise tizanidine levels.

**Don't stop suddenly.** The label warns that stopping tizanidine abruptly, especially after high doses or long use, can cause **rebound high blood pressure, a fast heart rate, and a return of muscle tightness**. Doctors usually taper the dose down gradually.

## What Actually Happens When You Mix Them

Effects vary a lot with your dose, how much you drink, your body size, your age, and whatever else you take. Here's a general picture, from the most common to the most serious.

### Common effects

- Much stronger drowsiness than usual, sometimes falling asleep without meaning to
- Dizziness and lightheadedness, worse when standing up
- Unsteadiness, clumsiness, and slow reactions
- Very dry mouth
- Feeling weak, heavy, or "wiped out"
- A rougher next morning, with grogginess that's hard to separate from a hangover

### More serious effects

- **Fainting**, usually when getting up, and the falls and injuries that come with it
- **A very slow heartbeat**, which can make you feel faint, short of breath, or confused
- **Confusion, vivid dreams, or hallucinations**, which the tizanidine label lists as possible side effects
- **Slowed or shallow breathing**, which becomes a real concern mainly when a third sedating drug such as an opioid or benzodiazepine is also involved

### Why the risk climbs fast with more drinks

Because alcohol raises tizanidine levels and stacks on its effects, the jump from "a bit sleepy" to "can't stand up safely" can happen sooner than you'd expect from your usual drink count. Someone who normally feels fine after two drinks may feel the way they'd usually feel after many more. That's also why driving after combining them is dangerous even if you think you feel okay. Our guide on [how long after drinking you can drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive) explains why feeling sober is a poor guide.

## Who Is at Higher Risk

Some people should be especially careful, and should talk to their prescriber before having any alcohol at all:

- **People taking blood pressure medicine.** Tizanidine plus an ACE inhibitor (such as lisinopril), a beta blocker, a diuretic ("water pill"), or another blood pressure drug can already drop pressure further. Alcohol adds a third push. Our guide to [lisinopril and alcohol](/never-hungover/lisinopril-and-alcohol) covers that piece of the puzzle.
- **Older adults.** They're more prone to blood pressure drops when standing, are more sensitive to sedation, and are more likely to be seriously hurt in a fall. Kidney function also tends to decline with age, and tizanidine is cleared more slowly when the kidneys work less well.
- **People with kidney problems.** The label notes that tizanidine is cleared much more slowly in people with significantly reduced kidney function, so doses are usually lowered.
- **People with liver problems,** because the liver breaks down tizanidine and both drugs can strain it.
- **Women taking birth control pills.** Oral contraceptives can slow how fast tizanidine is cleared, raising levels. Your prescriber usually accounts for this in your dose, but it's worth knowing when alcohol is in the picture.
- **People who've recently changed their smoking habits.** Smoking speeds up the enzyme that breaks down tizanidine. If you quit or cut back, tizanidine levels can rise. Mention any change to your prescriber.
- **Anyone on other sedating medicines**, covered in the next section.

## The Dangerous Combinations: When a Third Drug Is Involved

Tizanidine plus alcohol is risky. Tizanidine plus alcohol plus another sedating or blood pressure lowering drug is where serious harm becomes much more likely. If you take any of the following, have a direct conversation with your doctor or pharmacist about alcohol.

| Drug type | Examples | Why it matters with tizanidine and alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Opioids | Hydrocodone, oxycodone, tramadol, codeine | All three slow breathing and alertness; this is the most dangerous stack |
| Benzodiazepines | Alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), lorazepam | Strong added sedation and breathing risk |
| Gabapentinoids | Gabapentin, pregabalin (Lyrica) | Added drowsiness and dizziness; often prescribed alongside tizanidine |
| Other muscle relaxers | Cyclobenzaprine, baclofen, methocarbamol | More sedation; doctors rarely combine these on purpose |
| Sleep aids | Zolpidem (Ambien), diphenhydramine, doxylamine, trazodone | Added sedation, confusion, and fall risk at night |
| Blood pressure drugs | Lisinopril, amlodipine, metoprolol, diuretics | Bigger blood pressure drops and fainting |
| Other alpha-2 agonists | Clonidine, guanfacine | The label says not to combine with tizanidine |
| Strong CYP1A2 blockers | Fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin | Contraindicated; can multiply tizanidine levels several times over |

If you're taking an over-the-counter sleep aid or a "PM" painkiller, check the label. Many contain diphenhydramine or doxylamine, which are sedating antihistamines. Our guide to [sleep aids and alcohol](/never-hungover/sleep-aids-and-alcohol) has more on those.

Gabapentin deserves a special mention because it's so often prescribed together with tizanidine for nerve pain or spasticity. If that's your situation, our [gabapentin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) explains why the triple combination needs extra care.

## How Tizanidine Compares With Other Muscle Relaxers

People often get switched between muscle relaxers, and each one has its own alcohol issues. Our hub guide on [muscle relaxers and alcohol](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol) compares them all. Here's how tizanidine stacks up against the most common alternatives.

- **Cyclobenzaprine (Flexeril).** The most commonly prescribed muscle relaxer. It's chemically related to tricyclic antidepressants, causes a lot of drowsiness and dry mouth, and stays in the body for days. Its special concerns are heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome with some antidepressants. Tizanidine leaves the body much faster but has the bigger blood pressure effect. See our [cyclobenzaprine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/cyclobenzaprine-and-alcohol).
- **Baclofen.** The other main drug for spasticity. It acts on GABA, the same calming system alcohol affects, so the sedation overlap is strong. Like tizanidine, it must not be stopped suddenly. See our [baclofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/baclofen-and-alcohol).
- **Methocarbamol (Robaxin).** Generally considered one of the milder options for sedation, but it still adds to alcohol's effects. See our [methocarbamol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/methocarbamol-and-alcohol).

The point of this comparison isn't that one of them is fine with alcohol. None of them is. It's that the specific risks differ, and with tizanidine the one to watch most closely is your blood pressure.

## How Long Does Tizanidine Stay in Your System?

Tizanidine is a short-acting drug, which is one of the few pieces of good news here.

- **It starts working quickly.** Levels peak roughly one to two hours after a dose.
- **Its effects fade within hours.** Most people feel the main effects for about three to six hours, which is why it's often taken up to three times a day.
- **It clears fairly fast.** The label lists a half-life of about two and a half hours. A half-life is the time it takes for half the drug to leave your blood. It takes about five half-lives for a drug to mostly clear, which works out to roughly 12 to 15 hours for an average person.

That clearance time is longer in older adults and in people with kidney or liver problems, and it can be longer if you take a drug that blocks CYP1A2, including birth control pills.

### A practical way to think about timing

There's no official waiting period printed on the label, and the right answer depends on your dose and your health. Your prescriber or pharmacist is the person to set this for you. In general terms:

- **If you only take tizanidine occasionally,** such as one bedtime dose now and then, the drug is mostly gone by the next evening. Your prescriber can tell you whether a drink is reasonable after a set gap.
- **If you take it regularly, two or three times a day,** there's never really a gap when it's out of your system. Skipping a dose to make room for drinking isn't a fix, and stopping for several days at a time can bring on the rebound effects described below. This is exactly the situation where you need your prescriber's input before drinking.
- **The other direction matters too.** If you've been drinking, alcohol needs time to clear before you take your next dose. On average the body processes roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot. Our guide to [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) goes into the details.

## Don't Stop Tizanidine Just to Drink

This mistake is common enough to deserve its own section. If you take tizanidine regularly, especially at higher doses or for weeks or months, stopping abruptly can cause:

- A rebound rise in **blood pressure**
- A **fast heart rate**
- A return of **muscle stiffness and spasms**, sometimes worse than before

These rebound effects come from the same mechanism as clonidine withdrawal: your body has adjusted to the braking effect, and when the brake disappears suddenly, the system overshoots. Combine a rebound spike in blood pressure with a night of drinking and dehydration, and you've swapped one problem for another.

If you want to stop or cut back on tizanidine for any reason, including wanting to drink at an upcoming event, talk to your prescriber. They can tell you whether a short pause is safe for you or whether a gradual taper is needed.

## If You've Already Mixed Them

If you've had a drink or two and taken your usual dose, try not to panic. For many people the main effects will be extra sleepiness and dizziness that wear off as both drugs clear. Here's what to do:

1. **Sit or lie down, and stand up slowly.** When you get up, sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a minute first. If you feel lightheaded, sit back down.
2. **Don't drink any more alcohol,** and don't take another dose of tizanidine or any other sedating medicine.
3. **Drink some water.** Dehydration makes blood pressure drops worse.
4. **Don't drive, cycle, or operate anything dangerous** until both drugs have worn off.
5. **Don't be alone if you feel very drowsy or faint.** Let someone know what you took so they can keep an eye on you.
6. **Call your pharmacist or Poison Control** (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if you're unsure whether what you took is a problem. They can give advice for your specific doses.

> **Call 911 right away if someone:**
> - Faints and doesn't come round quickly, or keeps fainting
> - Is very hard to wake or can't stay awake
> - Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly
> - Has a very slow pulse, chest pain, or a pounding or irregular heartbeat
> - Is confused, agitated, or seeing things that aren't there
> - Has hit their head in a fall, even if they seem okay
>
> If the person also took an opioid, a benzodiazepine, or another sedating drug, take the situation even more seriously. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone.

## Practical Tips If Alcohol Is Part of Your Life

If you take tizanidine long term, alcohol is likely to come up at some point: holidays, weddings, dinners out. A few practical ideas:

- **Have the conversation before the event.** Ask your prescriber directly: "Is any alcohol okay with my dose, and if so, how should I time it?" Pharmacists are also great at this, and you don't need an appointment.
- **Know your dose schedule.** Your prescriber may suggest a specific plan around your doses. Don't invent your own by skipping or doubling doses.
- **Have alcohol-free options ready.** Non-alcoholic beer, wine, and mocktails are widely available and take the pressure off at social events.
- **Mind the bedtime window.** Tizanidine is often taken at night. Combining a bedtime dose with evening drinks puts the peak of both in the hours you're getting up to use the bathroom in the dark, which is a classic setup for falls.
- **Keep track of new prescriptions.** Any time a doctor prescribes something new, such as an antibiotic or antidepressant, mention that you take tizanidine. Ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine are off-limits, and several others need a dose change.

## Can DHM Help?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that we cover a lot on this site. Research, mostly in animals with limited human data, suggests it may support how the body processes alcohol and may ease some hangover symptoms.

To be clear about what it can't do: there's no good evidence that DHM reduces the interaction between tizanidine and alcohol, and it does not make the combination safe. It won't stop the blood pressure drop, the added sedation, or the rise in tizanidine levels. There's also a reason for caution, since some DHM research points to effects on the brain's GABA system, which many sedating drugs also act on. If you take tizanidine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM.

For people who aren't taking interacting medicines and want to try DHM on nights they do drink, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers which drugs to check first.

No supplement should change how you use a prescription medicine. Follow your prescription and your doctor's advice about alcohol, whatever else you take.

## The Bottom Line

- Tizanidine (Zanaflex) and alcohol both cause sedation and lower blood pressure, and alcohol also raises tizanidine levels in your blood. Together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, and fainting.
- The safest plan is to avoid alcohol while taking it, unless your prescriber has told you otherwise.
- Tizanidine clears from the body fairly quickly, roughly 12 to 15 hours for an average person, but longer with age, kidney or liver problems, and some other drugs.
- Don't stop tizanidine suddenly to make room for drinking. Rebound high blood pressure and a fast heart rate are real risks.
- The danger climbs sharply with a third drug: opioids, benzodiazepines, gabapentin, sleep aids, or blood pressure medicine. Fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin must never be taken with tizanidine.
- Call 911 if someone faints and doesn't recover quickly, is hard to wake, is breathing slowly, has a very slow or irregular heartbeat, or is confused.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking tizanidine?**

It's best not to. Tizanidine and alcohol both cause drowsiness and lower blood pressure, and the prescribing information reports that alcohol also raises tizanidine levels in the blood and increases its side effects. Together they can cause heavy sleepiness, dizziness, and fainting when you stand up. Ask your prescriber whether any alcohol is okay for you, and follow their limits.

**Is Zanaflex and alcohol the same as tizanidine and alcohol?**

Yes. Zanaflex is the brand name for tizanidine, and generic tizanidine tablets and capsules contain the same active drug. All of them carry the same alcohol warning.

**How long after taking tizanidine can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period on the label. Tizanidine has a half-life of about two and a half hours, so for an average person it mostly clears in roughly 12 to 15 hours. That time is longer for older adults, people with kidney or liver problems, and people taking drugs that slow its breakdown, including birth control pills. If you take tizanidine regularly, there's no real gap between doses, so talk to your prescriber before drinking.

**Can one drink on tizanidine hurt you?**

For many people, one drink will mainly make them sleepier and dizzier than usual. But the label doesn't set a safe amount, and even one drink can hit harder than expected, especially at the peak of a dose, in older adults, or alongside blood pressure medicine or another sedating drug. Fainting and falls are the main risk. Don't drive, and ask your prescriber whether any alcohol is reasonable for you.

**Why does tizanidine make you dizzy with alcohol?**

Tizanidine is related to clonidine, a blood pressure drug, and it lowers blood pressure and can slow the heart. Alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you, which also lowers blood pressure. Together, your blood pressure may not adjust when you stand up, causing lightheadedness, greying vision, or fainting. Stand up slowly and sit back down if you feel faint.

**Can I take tizanidine after drinking to help me sleep?**

It's not a good idea. Taking it at bedtime after drinking means both drugs peak while you're falling asleep and during the night, when you might get up and fall. Wait until the alcohol has cleared, or ask your pharmacist whether to skip that dose. Don't use tizanidine as a sleep aid after drinking.

**Should I stop taking tizanidine so I can drink?**

Not without talking to your prescriber. Stopping tizanidine suddenly, especially after regular use or higher doses, can cause rebound high blood pressure, a fast heart rate, and worse muscle stiffness. Your prescriber can tell you whether a short pause is safe or whether a gradual taper is needed.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on tizanidine?**

No. There's no good evidence that DHM reduces the interaction between tizanidine and alcohol, and it doesn't prevent the blood pressure drop or added sedation. Because some research suggests DHM acts on the brain's GABA system, check with your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with tizanidine or any other sedating medicine.
